gloss: An amount of money risked on the result of something uncertain.
examples: I made a small *bet* on the game.
He lost the *bet* and had to buy dinner.
Sports *bets* are legal in most states now.

gloss: A test version of a program released to users before the final version.
examples: The app is still in *beta*.
I signed up for the public *beta*.
Two *betas* shipped before the official launch.
contrast: Americans say BAY-tuh; British speakers say BEE-tuh.

gloss: An act of being disloyal to someone who trusted you.
examples: He never forgave that *betrayal*.
The letter felt like a *betrayal* of trust.
Her novels are full of small *betrayals*.

gloss: A feeling of being completely confused.
examples: She stared at the form in *bewilderment*.
His answer was met with total *bewilderment*.
There was a moment of *bewilderment* before anyone spoke.

gloss: A salt used in baking and as an antacid, known in the kitchen as baking soda.
examples: The label lists sodium *bicarbonate* as the main ingredient.
*Bicarbonate* neutralizes stomach acid.
Baking soda is just sodium *bicarbonate*.

gloss: The two-hundredth anniversary of an event.
examples: The town is planning a parade for its *bicentennial*.
The country celebrated its *bicentennial* in 1976.
Both cities marked their *bicentennials* the same summer.

gloss: The large muscle at the front of the upper arm.
examples: He tore his *biceps* lifting weights.
She flexed her *biceps* for the photo.
Curls work the *biceps* more than the shoulders.
contrast: The singular already ends in -s, and the plural is also biceps.

gloss: The offering of prices for something at an auction.
examples: *Bidding* starts at five hundred dollars.
The *bidding* went on for twenty minutes.
Online *bidding* closes Friday at noon.

gloss: Glasses whose lenses are divided into two parts, one for distance and one for reading.
examples: My dad finally got *bifocals*.
She pushed her *bifocals* up her nose.
A new pair of *bifocals* costs a few hundred dollars.
contrast: Always plural, like glasses and scissors: a pair of bifocals.

gloss: Someone who is stubbornly intolerant of people of other races, religions, or opinions.
examples: He called the caller a *bigot* and hung up.
The film shows how ordinary people become *bigots*.
Nobody wants to be seen as a *bigot*.

gloss: Stubborn intolerance toward people who are different.
examples: The speech was condemned as open *bigotry*.
She grew up surrounded by casual *bigotry*.
*Bigotry* has no place in this school.

gloss: The bitter greenish fluid made by the liver to help digest fat.
examples: The gallbladder stores *bile*.
*Bile* helps the body break down fats.
He was so sick he was throwing up *bile*.

gloss: The ability to speak two languages, or the use of two languages in a community.
examples: *Bilingualism* is common in border towns.
The study looked at the effects of early *bilingualism*.
The school has promoted *bilingualism* since kindergarten.

gloss: The number one thousand million, written 1,000,000,000.
examples: The company is worth over a *billion* dollars.
*Billions* of people watched the final.
The bridge cost half a *billion*.
contrast: In American English a billion is 1,000,000,000 — Russian миллиард, not «биллион».

gloss: Someone whose wealth is more than a billion dollars.
examples: A tech *billionaire* bought the newspaper.
The magazine ranks the world's *billionaires* every spring.
He became a *billionaire* at thirty-five.

gloss: A scientist who studies the chemistry of living things.
examples: She works as a *biochemist* at a drug company.
Two *biochemists* shared the prize.
The lab is hiring a *biochemist* this fall.

gloss: The study of the chemical processes inside living things.
examples: He's majoring in *biochemistry*.
The course covers basic *biochemistry*.
*Biochemistry* was her hardest class.

gloss: The variety of plant and animal life in a place.
examples: The reef has extraordinary *biodiversity*.
Logging threatens the region's *biodiversity*.
The park was created to protect *biodiversity*.

gloss: A writer who tells the story of another person's life.
examples: His *biographer* spent ten years on the book.
*Biographers* disagree about that period of her life.
She finally agreed to talk to the *biographer*.

gloss: A large natural region defined by its climate, plants, and animals.
examples: The desert *biome* covers much of the state.
Students compared three different *biomes*.
Tundra is the coldest *biome* on Earth.

gloss: The use of body measurements such as fingerprints or face scans to identify people.
examples: The airport uses *biometrics* at the gate.
*Biometrics* replaced the old ID cards.
Privacy groups have questions about *biometrics*.
contrast: Ends in -s but takes a singular verb: biometrics is faster than a passport check.

gloss: The removal of a small piece of tissue for medical testing.
examples: The doctor ordered a *biopsy*.
The *biopsy* came back clear.
He's had two *biopsies* this year.

gloss: The part of the earth where living things exist.
examples: Carbon moves between the atmosphere and the *biosphere*.
Pollution affects the entire *biosphere*.
The lecture explained how the *biosphere* recycles nitrogen.

ru: бёрди (в гольфе — на удар ниже пара)
gloss: A golf score of one stroke under par on a hole.
examples: She made a *birdie* on the last hole.
Three *birdies* in a row put him in the lead.
He needed a *birdie* to force a playoff.

gloss: A colored mark on the skin that has been there since birth.
examples: She has a small *birthmark* on her shoulder.
The laser treatment faded the *birthmark*.
Both twins have *birthmarks* in the same spot.

gloss: The place where someone was born, or where something began.
examples: The form asks for your *birthplace*.
The town calls itself the *birthplace* of jazz.
They visited the *birthplaces* of three presidents.

gloss: The number of babies born in a place over a period of time, counted per thousand people.
examples: The country's *birthrate* keeps falling.
*Birthrates* dropped sharply after the recession.
A low *birthrate* means fewer workers later on.

gloss: A right or possession someone has because of the family or country they were born into.
examples: Citizenship here is a *birthright*.
He said clean air should be every child's *birthright*.
The brothers argued over their *birthrights*.

gloss: A South Asian dish of spiced rice cooked with meat or vegetables.
examples: We ordered chicken *biryani* and naan.
Her *biryani* takes three hours to make.
The restaurant serves four different *biryanis*.

ru: бисквитная булочка (амер. мягкая булочка к завтраку)
gloss: A small soft bread roll served with butter or gravy, especially in the American South.
examples: We had *biscuits* and gravy for breakfast.
She makes *biscuits* from scratch every Sunday.
The fried chicken comes with a *biscuit*.
contrast: In American English a biscuit is a soft roll; a British "biscuit" is what Americans call a cookie.

gloss: A thick, creamy soup, usually made with shellfish.
examples: I ordered the lobster *bisque*.
The *bisque* was rich and a little too salty.
She's testing two tomato *bisques* for the menu.
contrast: Rhymes with "risk" — the -que is just a /k/ sound.

gloss: A dark board on a classroom wall that is written on with chalk.
examples: He wrote the date on the *blackboard*.
The old *blackboards* were replaced with whiteboards.
She erased the *blackboard* between classes.

gloss: A card game in which players try to get closer to twenty-one than the dealer.
examples: He plays *blackjack* every Friday night.
She learned *blackjack* from her uncle.
*Blackjack* gives you better odds than most casino games.

gloss: A list of people or things that are refused service, employment, or approval.
examples: His name ended up on a *blacklist*.
The agency keeps a *blacklist* of unsafe contractors.
Several *blacklists* circulated during those years.

gloss: Someone who makes and repairs iron objects by heating and hammering them.
examples: The village *blacksmith* shod horses.
He trained as a *blacksmith* after college.
Two *blacksmiths* gave demonstrations at the fair.

gloss: The black asphalt surface of a road, lot, or playground.
examples: The kids play basketball on the *blacktop*.
Fresh *blacktop* was laid over the summer.
The *blacktop* gets soft in the heat.
contrast: Everyday American word for asphalt paving; British English says "tarmac".

gloss: Responsibility for something bad that has happened.
examples: She took the *blame* for the mistake.
Don't put the *blame* on me.
There's plenty of *blame* to go around.

gloss: A mixture of two or more things combined together.
examples: This coffee is a *blend* of three beans.
The sweater is a wool and cotton *blend*.
The roaster sells several house *blends*.

gloss: A strip of cloth tied over someone's eyes so they cannot see.
examples: They put a *blindfold* on the birthday girl.
He took off the *blindfold* and looked around.
The game needs two *blindfolds*.

gloss: The condition of not being able to see.
examples: Diabetes is a leading cause of *blindness*.
The disease caused gradual *blindness*.
Color *blindness* runs in his family.

gloss: A quick shutting and opening of the eyes.
examples: It was over in the *blink* of an eye.
She answered without a single *blink*.
The test counts how many *blinks* you make per minute.

gloss: A small, temporary change or problem that does not last.
examples: The drop in sales was just a *blip*.
Analysts called the number a statistical *blip*.
There were a few *blips* in the data.

gloss: Perfect happiness.
examples: A hot shower after a long hike is pure *bliss*.
She smiled in complete *bliss*.
The first year of marriage was *bliss*.

gloss: A sudden, intense burst of effort or activity.
examples: The company launched an advertising *blitz*.
There was a media *blitz* before the election.
They did a cleaning *blitz* before the guests arrived.

gloss: A small shapeless drop or lump of something soft.
examples: There's a *blob* of ketchup on your shirt.
He squeezed a *blob* of toothpaste onto the brush.
*Blobs* of paint dried on the floor.

gloss: A group of countries, parties, or voters acting together for a common purpose.
examples: The trading *bloc* agreed on new tariffs.
Suburban voters are an important *bloc*.
Two rival *blocs* formed in the assembly.
contrast: Said exactly like "block", but a bloc is a political group and a block is a solid piece or a city street.

gloss: A movie, book, or product that is hugely successful.
examples: The studio needs a summer *blockbuster*.
Her novel became an instant *blockbuster*.
Three *blockbusters* open the same weekend.

gloss: A violent killing of many people, or a situation of severe losses.
examples: The battle turned into a *bloodbath*.
Monday's selloff was a *bloodbath* for tech stocks.
The layoffs were described as a *bloodbath*.

gloss: The killing or wounding of people, especially in a conflict.
examples: The talks ended without further *bloodshed*.
Both sides wanted to avoid *bloodshed*.
Years of *bloodshed* left the country exhausted.

gloss: A mark left on something by blood.
examples: There was a *bloodstain* on the carpet.
Investigators photographed the *bloodstains*.
The *bloodstain* wouldn't wash out.

gloss: The blood as it flows around the body.
examples: The drug goes straight into the *bloodstream*.
Alcohol enters the *bloodstream* within minutes.
The infection had spread to her *bloodstream*.

gloss: A hard hit, or a sudden shock or setback.
examples: He took a *blow* to the head.
Losing the contract was a serious *blow*.
The two fighters traded *blows* for three rounds.

gloss: A tool that makes a very hot flame for melting or burning things.
examples: He used a *blowtorch* to loosen the rusted bolt.
The chef finished the dessert with a *blowtorch*.
Two *blowtorches* were missing from the shop.

gloss: A fast style of American country music played on banjo, fiddle, and guitar.
examples: The festival is all *bluegrass* and barbecue.
He grew up playing *bluegrass* in Kentucky.
*Bluegrass* borrows a lot from old Irish tunes.

gloss: A careless and usually embarrassing mistake.
examples: Sending that email to everyone was a *blunder*.
The campaign never recovered from the *blunder*.
He made two *blunders* in the opening minutes.

gloss: The activity of traveling in a boat for pleasure.
examples: *Boating* is popular on the lake all summer.
They took a *boating* trip up the river.
The park allows *boating* and fishing.

gloss: A wild North American cat with a short tail and spotted fur.
examples: A *bobcat* crossed the road in front of us.
*Bobcats* hunt rabbits at dawn.
The trail camera caught a *bobcat* last night.

gloss: A fast racing sled that a team steers down an icy track.
examples: Their *bobsled* set a track record.
He drove a four-man *bobsled* at the Olympics.
The *bobsleds* are stored at the bottom of the run.
contrast: Americans say bobsled; the British and international word is bobsleigh.

gloss: A small neighborhood grocery store, especially in a city.
examples: I grabbed a sandwich at the *bodega* on the corner.
The *bodega* is open until two in the morning.
There are three *bodegas* on this block.

gloss: Someone who develops large muscles through weight training.
examples: He trains like a *bodybuilder*.
The *bodybuilders* posed on stage.
She's a competitive *bodybuilder*.

gloss: The sport of building large muscles through weight training.
examples: He got into *bodybuilding* in high school.
*Bodybuilding* takes years of steady work.
She quit *bodybuilding* after an injury.

gloss: Someone hired to protect a person from attack.
examples: The singer travels with two *bodyguards*.
His *bodyguard* waited by the door.
She works as a *bodyguard* for executives.

gloss: An imaginary frightening figure used to scare children, or anything people are taught to fear.
examples: He was sure the *bogeyman* was under his bed.
Immigration became the campaign's *bogeyman*.
Every generation invents new *bogeymen*.
contrast: Also spelled boogeyman in American English; both spellings are said the same way.

gloss: Standard wording reused without change in contracts, documents, or code.
examples: Most of the contract is just *boilerplate*.
Skip the *boilerplate* and read clause nine.
He pasted in the usual legal *boilerplate*.

gloss: Willingness to take risks and act with confidence.
examples: Her *boldness* surprised the committee.
The plan was praised for its *boldness*.
It took *boldness* to say that out loud.

gloss: A continuous heavy attack with bombs or shells.
examples: The city survived weeks of *bombardment*.
The *bombardment* began before dawn.
Repeated *bombardments* destroyed the bridge.
contrast: The last b in "bomb" is silent, but the second b in bombardment is pronounced.

gloss: An attack in which a bomb is dropped or set off.
examples: The *bombing* injured six people.
Police are investigating a string of *bombings*.
The *bombing* of the bridge cut the city in two.
contrast: The b of the root is silent: BAH-ming, not "bomb-ing".

gloss: A piece of shocking, completely unexpected news.
examples: The report dropped a *bombshell*.
Her resignation was a *bombshell*.
The hearing produced two *bombshells* in one afternoon.

gloss: The forming of a close emotional connection between people.
examples: The trip was good *bonding* for the team.
Skin-to-skin contact helps *bonding* after birth.
They call it a *bonding* exercise.

gloss: A soft hat tied under the chin, worn especially by babies.
examples: The baby wore a white *bonnet*.
She kept her grandmother's Easter *bonnet*.
The girls' *bonnets* blew off in the wind.
contrast: In British English a bonnet is also the hood of a car; Americans say hood.

gloss: The work of keeping records of the money a business receives and spends.
examples: She does the *bookkeeping* for two small shops.
Sloppy *bookkeeping* got the company in trouble.
*Bookkeeping* software saves hours every month.
contrast: One of the few English words with three double letters in a row: oo-kk-ee.

gloss: A small thin book with a paper cover that gives information.
examples: The *booklet* explains how to fill out the form.
They handed out *booklets* at the door.
There's a safety *booklet* in the seat pocket.

gloss: Someone who loves reading and reads a great deal.
examples: She's been a *bookworm* since she was six.
The library is full of *bookworms* on rainy days.
My son is a total *bookworm*.

gloss: A period of rapid growth in business, building, or population.
examples: The town grew fast during the oil *boom*.
A housing *boom* pushed prices up.
The industry has been through several *booms* and busts.

gloss: A curved wooden stick that comes back to the person who throws it.
examples: He threw the *boomerang* and it came right back.
The museum shop sells painted *boomerangs*.
A *boomerang* is harder to throw than it looks.

gloss: An increase or improvement that helps something.
examples: The win gave the team a *boost*.
Coffee gives me a quick *boost* in the morning.
Two rate cuts gave the market small *boosts*.

gloss: A person or company that takes a loan and has to pay it back.
examples: The *borrower* has thirty years to repay the loan.
Rates are higher for first-time *borrowers*.
Many *borrowers* refinanced when rates fell.

gloss: A scientist who studies plants.
examples: A *botanist* identified the plant from a photo.
*Botanists* found a new species in the canyon.
She became a *botanist* after studying forestry.

gloss: The scientific study of plants.
examples: She took *botany* her sophomore year.
The book is a classic of American *botany*.
*Botany* was once required for medical students.

gloss: The lowest part or surface of something.
examples: The keys were at the *bottom* of my bag.
Write your name at the *bottom* of the page.
The *bottoms* of the pots were burned.

gloss: A dangerous kind of food poisoning caused by bacteria in badly preserved food.
examples: Home canning done wrong can cause *botulism*.
Three cases of *botulism* were traced to the same soup.
*Botulism* is rare but very serious.

gloss: A large branch of a tree.
examples: Snow weighed down the *boughs*.
A heavy *bough* cracked and fell.
They decorated the mantel with pine *boughs*.
contrast: The gh is silent — it rhymes with "cow" and sounds just like "bow" (to bend forward).

gloss: A clear broth, or the dried cube of it used to flavor cooking.
examples: Drop a *bouillon* cube into the boiling water.
The soup starts with chicken *bouillon*.
She keeps beef *bouillon* in the pantry.
contrast: Close in sound to "bullion" (bars of gold), but bouillon is soup.

gloss: A movement back up or away after hitting a surface.
examples: Catch it on the first *bounce*.
The ball took a bad *bounce*.
The trampoline gave him a few huge *bounces*.

gloss: A line marking the limit of an area, or a limit on what is acceptable.
examples: The fence marks the *boundary* between the two farms.
Good friendships need clear *boundaries*.
The river forms the county *boundary*.

gloss: A reward offered for catching someone or for getting rid of something.
examples: The state pays a *bounty* for each wild hog.
There's a *bounty* on his head.
Tech companies pay *bounties* for security bugs.

gloss: A short period of something unpleasant, such as an illness.
examples: She's getting over a *bout* of the flu.
He had another *bout* of insomnia.
Two *bouts* of bad weather delayed the harvest.

gloss: A single flower worn in the buttonhole of a jacket.
examples: The groom wore a white *boutonniere*.
He pinned on a *boutonniere* before the prom.
The florist made matching *boutonnieres*.
contrast: A French word: the final -re is said NEER, not "nee-air".

gloss: A refusal to buy from or deal with a company or country as a protest.
examples: Shoppers organized a *boycott* of the chain.
The *boycott* lasted eleven months.
Consumer *boycotts* rarely last long.

gloss: A man or boy someone is romantically involved with.
examples: She brought her *boyfriend* to dinner.
They've been *boyfriend* and girlfriend since high school.
Her last two *boyfriends* both moved away.

gloss: The time of a man's life when he was a boy.
examples: He spent his *boyhood* on a farm in Iowa.
The house holds all his *boyhood* memories.
*Boyhood* friendships can last a lifetime.

gloss: A support worn on part of the body to hold it in place while it heals.
examples: He wore a knee *brace* all season.
The doctor fitted her with a back *brace*.
Two ankle *braces* are in the gym bag.
